newsitem.title: ITALY: Fiat's Romiti adds voice to attacks on Italy govt.
newsitem.headline: Fiat's Romiti adds voice to attacks on Italy govt.

text.p: Cesare Romiti, chairman of Italian car giant Fiat, added his weight to industry's criticism of the government on Monday, backing the head of the employers' federation who said Rome was not doing enough to help business.
Romiti, in an interview with La Repubblica newspaper, said Confindustria president Giorgio Fossa might have overstated his position, but said the position itself was correct.
"Fossa could have exaggerated in expressing himself. It is a problem of language," Romiti was quoted as saying. "But there is no doubt that in substance, he is right...that is what counts."
Fossa told a business convention in Milan on Saturday: "If the government doesn't change course, the country itself will sweep it away."
Fossa criticised the centre-left government of Prime Minister Romano Prodi for increasing taxes in the 1997 budget and said companies needed incentives to create new jobs.

Romiti also said Prodi's budget package, currently before parliament, was too heavily weighted with taxes. The budget aims to cut 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's deficit and levy a "Euro-tax" to help Italy meet criteria to be among founding members of a single European currency in 1999.

"The government, above all else, needs to inspire hope in Italians," Romiti said. "It's not enough to say, wait until 1999 when we will enter Europe. We are already at the end of 1996 and we need something more, something more immediate.
"It is necessary to truly relaunch the economy, stem the rising fear over unemployment, support trade and industry..."

Auto sector research bodies have called on the government to help the depressed Italian car market, but Prodi said at the weekend the government had no intention of introducing incentives to boost flagging sales.

Foreign Trade Minister Augusto Fantozzi also stepped into the debate on Monday. He told La Stampa newspaper in an that Fossa was wrong to attack the government's programme, saying it undermined efforts to help Italian companies.
Fantozzi was interviewed in Singapore where he will attend this week's meeting of the World Trade Organisation.

"The government does not risk being crushed by public opinion if the public has the patience to wait for budget measures which must balance the sacrifices which have been imposed on the public so far," Fantozzi said.
"After Italy has entered Europe..., we will need to reduce the fiscal pressure in favour of development," he added.
